item.title: §3.1.2 Competence
item.description:
1. Clause Overview

For an open source program to actually function, the people assigned to relevant roles must have the competence to perform those roles. If roles and responsibilities are only written in documents and the people responsible have no basic knowledge of open source license or security vulnerability management, the policies and processes will be nominal. §3.1.2 requires the organization to identify the roles involved in the program, define the competence required for each role, evaluate and record whether participants actually possess that competence. This clause advances the role structure defined in §3.1.1 Policy into a concrete competence framework.

item.title: §4.1.2 Competence
item.description:
★ 18974 Exclusive Items — Documented Evidence Strength

§4.1.2.3·§4.1.2.5·§4.1.2.6 are ISO 18974 exclusive (★) items requiring Documented Evidence. A simple procedure document is insufficient — you must retain actual execution records (participant list, review meeting minutes, internal best practice comparison results). For a detailed explanation of the strength difference, see §4.1.5 Standard Practices — Documented Evidence Notice.

1. Clause Overview

§4.1.2 has the same basic structure as ISO/IEC 5230 §3.1.2 (Competence), but requires 3 additional Verification Material items. While 5230 requires three items — a list of roles, a definition of competencies per role, and evidence of competency assessment — 18974 additionally requires a list of participants and their role mappings (4.1.2.3), evidence of periodic review and process changes (4.1.2.5), and verification of alignment with internal best practices (4.1.2.6). These three additional items require demonstrating that the competence framework is not merely formal, but is actively kept up to date and aligned with industry standards.

item.title: 3.2 Competence
item.description:
Implementation phase

This clause is implemented in Phase 1: Program Foundation. View the full implementation roadmap

1. Clause Overview

If the policy (3.1) sets out what must be done, competence ensures there are people who can do it. AI SBOM compliance requires broader knowledge than open source compliance, which dealt only with code licenses. Practitioners must judge the licenses of model weights and datasets, interpret model cards, and understand emerging AI regulations and the use restrictions of non-standard licenses.

ISO/IEC 42001 §7 covers the competence, awareness, communication, and documentation needed to operate the AI management system. From the perspective of open source practitioners, §7.2 (Competence) and §7.5 (Documented information) are the key points of intersection.
